content: Studies conducted on newborn animals and pilot studies in humans have indicated that mild hypothermia administered after peripartum hypoxia-ischemia in newborns may reduce neurological complications without causing harmful side effects. The objective of this research was to evaluate the impact of therapeutic hypothermia on mortality, long-term neurodevelopmental disabilities, and clinically significant side effects in newborns with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group's standard strategy. This included databases such as the Oxford Database of Perinatal Trials, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and MEDLINE, covering studies from 1966 to June 2007. Additional sources included prior reviews, conference proceedings, expert consultations, and manual journal searches. The search was updated in May 2012. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials comparing therapeutic hypothermia with standard care in term or late preterm infants who had evidence of peripartum asphyxia and moderate-to-severe encephalopathy, excluding those with major congenital anomalies. The primary outcome assessed was the combined rate of death or long-term major neurodevelopmental disability. Secondary outcomes included adverse effects of cooling and early indicators of neurodevelopmental outcomes. Four independent reviewers assessed the quality of the studies, extracted data, and contacted study authors for additional information. Meta-analyses were performed using risk ratios (RR), risk differences (RD), and weighted mean differences for continuous data, all with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The updated review included 11 randomized controlled trials involving 1,505 term and late preterm infants with moderate-to-severe encephalopathy and evidence of intrapartum asphyxia. Therapeutic hypothermia significantly reduced the combined outcome of mortality or major neurodevelopmental disability by 18 months of age. The typical risk ratio (RR) was 0.75 (95% CI 0.68 to 0.83), and the risk difference (RD) was -0.15 (95% CI -0.20 to -0.10). The number needed to treat for one additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) was 7 (95% CI 5 to 10) based on data from eight studies involving 1,344 infants. Cooling also led to a significant reduction in mortality alone, with a typical RR of 0.75 (95% CI 0.64 to 0.88) and an RD of -0.09 (95% CI -0.13 to -0.04). The NNTB for mortality reduction was 11 (95% CI 8 to 25) based on data from 11 studies involving 1,468 infants. Among survivors, therapeutic hypothermia reduced the risk of neurodevelopmental disability, with a typical RR of 0.77 (95% CI 0.63 to 0.94) and an RD of -0.13 (95% CI -0.19 to -0.07). The NNTB for reducing neurodevelopmental disability was 8 (95% CI 5 to 14) based on data from eight studies involving 917 infants. Adverse effects associated with therapeutic hypothermia included an increased incidence of sinus bradycardia and a significant rise in thrombocytopenia. In conclusion, evidence from these 11 randomized controlled trials demonstrates that therapeutic hypothermia is beneficial for term and late preterm newborns with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy. Cooling reduces mortality and does not increase the risk of major disabilities in survivors. The benefits of therapeutic hypothermia in terms of survival and neurodevelopmental outcomes outweigh the short-term adverse effects. It is recommended that hypothermia be initiated in term and late preterm infants with moderate-to-severe hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy within six hours of birth. Further research is needed to refine the techniques of cooling, including patient selection, duration of therapy, and methods of delivering therapeutic hypothermia.
